extracted.intended_audience: university technology transfer offices, campus export-compliance officers, university researchers and counsel involved in technology transfer and patenting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for university technology transfer offices and researchers to ensure transfers of materials, items, and technical information comply with U.S. export controls, BPARA, USA PATRIOT Act, OFAC sanctions, and related regulatory regimes — including interactions with patenting and research dissemination. Emphasis on when licenses are required, applicable exclusions, and procedural safeguards before contracting or transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with applicable U.S. transfer-related laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The receiver of the subject materials will comply with all applicable U.S. laws and regulations relating to the transfer, acquisition, receipt, possession, shipping, and/or transport of the materials, including without limitation BPARA and USA PATRIOT Act, to the extent applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contracts/agreements require recipients to comply with applicable statutes and implementing regulations (e.g., BPARA, USA PATRIOT Act); confirm obligations before transfer. Consult cited authorities (e.g., CDC FAQ) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult BPARA responsible official before biological-material agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where biological materials are being transferred or received, the technology transfer office should confer with the institution’s BPARA responsible official prior to entering the relevant agreement to determine whether the materials are regulated by BPARA or by Section 817(2) of the USA PATRIOT Act, and to determine whether the prerequisites to the transfer have been met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine regulatory status early in negotiations; the BPARA official can advise whether registration, certifications, or specific transfer procedures are required before executing MTAs/TTAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered biologicals require institution-arranged transfers and regulatory satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: If covered biologicals are involved, the institution’s BPARA responsible official will need to arrange for the transfer, and the transferring and receiving institutions will need to satisfy the regulatory requirement before the transfer is initiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not initiate physical transfers of covered agents until registration/certificates and any prerequisites are in place; document compliance steps and approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate with campus export-compliance office and export-control experts
rubrics_metrics.description: The technology transfer office should coordinate with the office that administers the institution’s export-compliance program and its expert in export controls, as well as with the inventors, to ensure that the technology transfer process does not contribute to a violation of export controls or embargoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve export-control specialists and inventors at an early stage (before contracting or committing to transfers) to evaluate licensing needs, exclusions, and risk of facilitating violations via MTAs or technical assistance agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish materials/items from technical information for control analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Export controls apply to many types of equipment, chemicals, biological agents and toxins, materials, goods, and software code (materials or items) and to certain information, training, and instruction relating to controlled materials or items. If only technical information, not materials or items, is involved in a proposed transfer or disclosure to anyone abroad or to a foreign national in the U.S., it is easier to first consider whether the fundamental research, publicly available/public domain, or another exclusion from controls applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed transfer involves physical materials/items (higher scrutiny) or only information (may qualify for exclusions). When materials are involved, expect more rigorous licensing analysis and potential prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand principal U.S. export-control regimes (ITAR, EAR, OFAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The three principal export control and embargo regimes in the United States are the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) of the State Department, the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) of the Commerce Department, and the regulations of the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the Treasury Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate transfers under each regime as applicable: ITAR for defense articles/services/technical data; EAR for dual-use commercial/military items and technologies; OFAC for embargoes/sanctions. All three can apply concurrently and have different scopes and licensing authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: EAR scope and Commerce Control List (CCL)
rubrics_metrics.description: EAR generally governs exports of materials or items that may have a dual use ... EAR lists the items subject to its regulation on the Commerce Control List (CCL), which includes a catchall category, EAR 99.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether items/technology appear on the CCL or fall under EAR99; a technical and regulatory analysis is often required to classify items and determine licensing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: ITAR scope and U.S. Munitions List (USML)
rubrics_metrics.description: ITAR generally governs exports of defense articles, related technical data and defense services that are 'specifically designed, developed, configured, adapted, or modified for a military application' or have significant military or intelligence applicability; many regulated items are listed on the United States Munitions List (USML).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even innocuous-seeming equipment may be ITAR-controlled depending on configuration (example: mini research submersibles). If ITAR applies, the State Department/DDTC is the licensing authority; treat technical data and services as controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFAC embargoes/sanctions may independently bar transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: OFAC regulations govern payments to, transfers of any service, materials, or items of value to, or travel to, certain sanctioned and embargoed foreign countries, and transactions with and transfers to certain embargoed individual and entity end users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult OFAC lists before any transaction; OFAC prohibitions can block transfers even when EAR/ITAR exclusions would otherwise apply. An OFAC general license does not obviate EAR/ITAR licensing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of export and the scope of information transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: An export under EAR and ITAR is the transfer outside of the United States or to a foreign embassy of any controlled materials or items ... An export also includes the disclosure abroad of any controlled software, or of controlled technologies or technical data ... regardless of the medium in which such information is transmitted (oral, visual, electronic, wire, radio, or physical conveyance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any communication of controlled technical data to persons abroad as an export irrespective of medium; plan licensing/controls accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prevalence of deemed exports on campuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Deemed exports are the transfer or disclosure, visually, electronically, or in any other medium, of controlled software or technologies or technical data to a foreign entity or individual in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that disclosures to foreign students, visiting scholars, or employees in the U.S. can constitute deemed exports; include these scenarios in compliance screening and licensing assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain required EAR/ITAR licenses when no exclusion applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless an exclusion from regulation applies, before any export or deemed export of materials or items (or of related information constituting technical data or technologies) regulated under ITAR may occur, and before some such exports or deemed exports regulated under EAR may occur, a license must be obtained from the relevant agency, DDTC, or BIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not send controlled materials or technical information abroad or disclose to foreign nationals in the U.S. without confirming an applicable exclusion or securing the necessary license(s). Licenses can take months and may be denied; obtain confirmation before contracting to transfer or disclosing information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export documentation required even when license not required
rubrics_metrics.description: When an EAR or ITAR license is not required for controlled materials or items, and when an export is exempt from licensing, export documentation is still required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain proper export paperwork and recordkeeping even when relying on exclusions or exemptions; documentation supports compliance and auditability.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFAC screening before contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Before any contract is entered into for the transfer of materials or items or related information, or for the provision of any payment, advice, or service, OFAC sanctions lists should be consulted to ensure that the transfer is not to a prohibited person, entity, or country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the transfer targets a prohibited party, do not proceed without an OFAC license; evaluate likelihood of obtaining OFAC license based on sanction scope and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental research and publicly available/public domain exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two exclusions most relevant in a technology transfer context are the fundamental research exclusion (based on NSDD 189: 'basic and applied research ... the results of which ordinarily are published and shared broadly within the scientific community') and the publicly available/public domain exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether research meets NSDD 189 prerequisites (open dissemination, no proprietary restrictions). These exclusions more readily apply to information than to materials/items. Government and agency guidance (NSDD 189) remains policy; confirm applicability with export experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on dissemination may destroy export-control exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrictions and other conditions limiting access to and dissemination of research results under material transfer and license agreements may arguably destroy the fundamental research and public availability/public domain exclusions from export controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contractual terms that effectively make research proprietary or limit dissemination if relying on these exclusions; research licenses that allow unrestricted sublicenses for research use may preserve exclusions. Consult expert counsel when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting interactions with exclusions — choose and satisfy prerequisites carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is the individual’s or institution’s intention to patent export-controlled intellectual property that also is sought to be covered by an exclusion from EAR and ITAR, careful consideration must be given on how to accomplish both objectives and which exclusion to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify IP for patent protection without forfeiting necessary exclusions, ensure prerequisites are met (e.g., for fundamental research, foreign nationals may need to receive controlled information only on campus). Coordinate patenting strategy with export-compliance analysis to avoid losing export exclusions or patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-filed disclosures for prosecution abroad — limited exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Transferring export-controlled information to a foreign jurisdiction as part of a technology disclosure in order to seek patent protection in that jurisdiction does not require an EAR or ITAR license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume broad freedom to export patent-related information: transfers of the same information abroad for other purposes, or in the U.S. to a foreign national before the patent is published, may require licenses depending on controls and nationalities involved. Evaluate case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of violations and institutional risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation of export controls and embargoes can carry significant criminal and civil penalties against the individual involved as well as against the institution. The possibility of losing export privileges and of damage to an institution’s reputation are also significant penalties for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor potential criminal/civil exposure, loss of export privileges, and reputational harm into decision-making; adopt conservative compliance practices, training, and documentation to mitigate institutional risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Export status independent of recipient's U.S. citizenship for physical exports; travel caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: When export controls apply, they apply to U.S.-origin materials or items and certain related information, training, and instruction, wherever they are located or take place... It does not matter for purposes of defining export whether the recipient abroad is a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident or is a foreign national. The mere travel abroad by an individual whose personal knowledge includes controlled technical data/technologies, however, is not an export as long as the controlled information is not communicated to anyone abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen transactions on destination and end-user basis rather than relying on recipient citizenship for physical exports. Train staff to recognize that personal travel with knowledge is not a substitute for a license if disclosure occurs.
